candidates.title: Heterogeneity of Treatment Effect of ABC Pathway-Based Care in Older Atrial Fibrillation: Insights from the mAFA-II and MIRACLE-AF Trials Using a Causal Machine Learning Approach.
candidates.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Integrated care based on the Atrial fibrillation Better Care (ABC) pathway improves outcomes in patients with atrial fibrillation (AF), but whether treatment effects differ across older patients remains unclear.
OBJECTIVES: To evaluate heterogeneity of treatment effect (HTE) of ABC pathway-based care and assess its transportability across healthcare settings using causal machine learning (ML).
METHODS: Individual participant data from the cluster-randomised mAFA-II and MIRACLE-AF trials were analysed, including 3,209 patients aged ≥65 years. Three causal ML models were developed in mAFA-II and externally validated in MIRACLE-AF. The primary outcome was a composite of all-cause mortality, ischaemic stroke, intracranial haemorrhage, heart failure, acute coronary syndrome, or major bleeding.
RESULTS: The uplift random forest demonstrated the best performance and identified meaningful HTE. In the mAFA-II testing cohort, ABC pathway-based care was associated with a lower risk of the primary outcome in patients predicted to benefit, whereas no benefit and possible harm were observed in those predicted to derive harm (P-interaction=0.002). In external validation, benefit was preserved in the predicted benefit group but not in the predicted harm group, although treatment discrimination was attenuated. Patients predicted to derive limited benefit had greater clinical complexity, including higher comorbidity burden and CHA2DS2-VASc scores. Sex, heart failure, and hypertension were the strongest predictors of treatment effect.
CONCLUSIONS: ABC pathway-based integrated care demonstrates clinically meaningful treatment heterogeneity among older patients with AF. These findings support more personalised implementation of integrated care and highlight the potential of causal ML to guide precision management in AF.
CLINICAL TRIAL REGISTRATION: MAFA-II trial (ChiCTR-OOC-17014138 || http://www.chictr.org.cn/, registered on 26 December 2017), MIRACLE-AF trial (NCT04622514 || https://clinicaltrials.gov/, registered on 10 November 2020).

candidates.title: Not All PVR Reductions Are Created Equal: Lessons From the CADENCE Trial.
candidates.abstract: The CADENCE trial evaluated sotatercept in combined post- and pre-capillary pulmonary hypertension associated with heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (CpcPH-HFpEF). We analyzed the pathophysiological implications of the observed pulmonary vascular resistance (PVR) reduction.A hemodynamic comparison was conducted contrasting the mechanistic effects of sotaercept with conventional pulmonary vasodilators.In CADENCE, PVR and pressure reductions occurred without marked cardiac output augmentation, contrasting with flow-mediated recruitment typical of traditional vasodilators. Sotatercept-induced PVR reduction may reflect true vascular reverse remodeling rather than vasodilation, underscoring the need to discriminate resistance reduction mechanisms in CpcPHHFpEF.

candidates.title: Systemic Hypertension and Survival in Pulmonary Hypertension.
candidates.abstract:
IMPORTANCE: Pulmonary hypertension (PH), a progressive and life-threatening condition with rising prevalence among older adults, frequently coexists with systemic hypertension, the prognostic impact of which is poorly understood.
OBJECTIVE: To evaluate the association between systemic hypertension and survival in patients with PH.
DESIGN, SETTING, AND PARTICIPANTS: This multicenter cohort study analyzed data from the Pulmonary Vascular Research Institute GoDeep meta-registry, integrating global retrospective and prospective PH cohorts (n = 3238 in Europe, n = 3014 in North America, n = 96 in Africa, n = 802 in Asia, and n = 851 in Oceania). Survival was assessed using multivariable Cox proportional hazards models and adjusted for key confounders, with sensitivity analyses to validate robustness. Independent external validation was performed in a cohort in the UK. A total of 12 771 patients with incident PH (median [IQR] age, 65 [53-73] years; 7372 [58%] female) were diagnosed via right heart catheterization and comprehensive clinical data, encompassing PH groups 1-5 and all age categories. The study spans diagnosis decades from 1980 to 2020. Data were analyzed from February 2025 until September 2026.
EXPOSURES: Center-reported diagnosis of systemic hypertension, baseline systolic systemic arterial pressure (sSAP), and heart rate as well as longitudinal sSAP and heart rate trajectories.
MAIN OUTCOMES AND MEASURES: All-cause mortality, adjusted for confounding variables, including age, PH group, antihypertensive and PH-specific medications, and cardiac index.
RESULTS: Higher baseline sSAP and preexisting systemic hypertension were independently associated with improved survival. Patients with hypertension exhibited a 26% reduced mortality hazard (hazard ratio [HR], 0.74; 95% CI, 0.68-0.79) compared to their counterparts without hypertension. Survival benefits correlated positively with increasing sSAP (80-180 mm Hg), remained consistent across PH groups and age groups, and were independent of antihypertensive and PH-specific medications. Elevated heart rate was associated with higher mortality. sSAP increments correlated with improved cardiac index and tricuspid annular plane systolic excursion. Decreased sSAP and higher heart rate during follow-up correlated with higher mortality. External validation in a separate UK cohort confirmed these findings.
CONCLUSION AND RELEVANCE: In this global PH cohort, higher sSAP was associated with enhanced survival, while a higher baseline heart rate and declining systemic blood pressure during follow-up were significantly associated with increased mortality risk.

candidates.title: N-Acetylgalactosamine-Conjugated Small Interfering RNA Targeting Hepatic Angiotensinogen in Hypertension: A Phase I Clinical Trial With Randomized Part A and Open-Label Part B.
candidates.abstract:
IMPORTANCE: Angiotensinogen (AGT) is the precursor of angiotensin peptides and a key determinant of renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system activity. ART101 is an investigational N-acetylgalactosamine-conjugated small interfering RNA (GalNAc-siRNA) designed to durably suppress hepatic AGT synthesis.
OBJECTIVE: To evaluate the safety, tolerability, pharmacokinetics, and pharmacodynamics of single ascending doses of the AGT-targeting GalNAc-siRNA in healthy volunteers and to provide an initial exploratory assessment of blood pressure effects in patients with hypertension.
DESIGN, SETTING, AND PARTICIPANTS: This phase I study was conducted from January 2025 to April 2026 with 24-week follow-up. Part A was a double-blind, placebo-controlled, single ascending-dose trial; part B was an open-label, single-dose study. The study took place at Beijing Friendship Hospital, Capital Medical University, Beijing, China. Part A enrolled 40 healthy adults randomized 6:2 to receive the GalNAc-siRNA (25-600 mg) or placebo; 39 completed the study. Part B enrolled 8 patients with hypertension receiving the GalNAc-siRNA, 600 mg; all completed the study.
INTERVENTIONS: A single subcutaneous injection of the AGT-targeting GalNAc-siRNA (25, 75, 150, 300, or 600 mg) or placebo in part A; a single open-label subcutaneous injection of GalNAc-siRNA, 600 mg, in part B.
MAIN OUTCOMES AND MEASURES: The primary outcome was safety and tolerability; secondary outcomes included pharmacokinetics, pharmacodynamics, exploratory blood pressure assessments, and renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system biomarkers.
RESULTS: Among 40 healthy volunteers (27 [67.5%] male; mean [SD] age, 40.4 [7.8] years) and 8 patients (6 [75.0%] male; mean [SD] age, 47.3 [10.3] years) with hypertension, the AGT-targeting GalNAc-siRNA was well tolerated. In part A, treatment-emergent adverse events (TEAEs) occurred in 23 of 30 active-treatment participants (76.7%) vs 7 of 10 placebo recipients (70.0%); in part B, 6 of 8 patients (75.0%) had TEAEs. No serious adverse events, injection site reactions, or hyperkalemia were observed; all TEAEs were mild to moderate. Plasma exposure (maximum plasma concentration [Cmax] and area under the plasma concentration-time curve [AUC]) increased with dose over the wide dose range from 25 mg to 600 mg. Mean maximum serum AGT reductions of 93% (at 600 mg) in healthy volunteers and 90% (at 600 mg) in patients with hypertension were observed. At 24 weeks after a single 600-mg dose, the placebo-corrected 24-hour ambulatory systolic blood pressure decreased by 12.9 mm Hg in healthy participants.
CONCLUSION AND RELEVANCE: In this phase I study, no serious treatment-related safety signals were identified. Sustained, dose-dependent AGT reductions and exploratory blood pressure lowering were observed. These findings support further investigation of the AGT-targeting GalNAc-siRNA as a potential long-acting therapeutic for hypertension.
TRIAL REGISTRATION: China Drug Clinical Registry Identifiers: CTR20250041 (part A) and CTR20253973 (part B).

candidates.title: Intensive vs More Intensive Lipid-Lowering Therapy and Plaque Regression in Statin-Naive Patients: Prespecified Analyses From the FLOWPROMOTE Randomized Clinical Trial.
candidates.abstract:
IMPORTANCE: Prior imaging studies (predominantly using intravascular ultrasound) have demonstrated modest plaque regression with lipid-lowering therapy in stable coronary artery disease (CAD). The effect of initiating intensive lipid-lowering therapy on coronary plaque regression across the entire coronary tree in treatment-naive patients remains uncertain.
OBJECTIVE: To report the prespecified secondary imaging end points of the FLOWPROMOTE trial by comparing the effects of intensive vs more intensive lipid-lowering therapy on plaque regression in statin-naive patients with stable CAD and to assess the association between achieved low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C) levels and plaque regression.
DESIGN, SETTING, AND PARTICIPANTS: FLOWPROMOTE was a multicenter randomized clinical trial enrolling statin-naive patients with newly diagnosed stable CAD, defined by a coronary computed tomography angiography (CTA) stenosis greater than 50% and fractional flow reserve CT less than or equal to 0.80. Coronary CTA was performed at baseline and repeated at 9 and 18 months. Study data were analyzed from February 2025 to January 2026.
INTERVENTIONS: Patients were randomized to intensive lipid-lowering therapy (atorvastatin 40 mg) or more intensive lipid-lowering therapy (rosuvastatin 40 mg plus ezetimibe 10 mg) for 18 months.
MAIN OUTCOMES AND MEASURES: Prespecified secondary end points included changes in total plaque volume (TPV), noncalcified plaque volume (NCPV), and calcified plaque volume (CPV) across all coronary vessels at 9 and 18 months compared with baseline.
RESULTS: A total of 104 patients (mean [SD] age, 64 [9] years; 82 male [79%]) were included in this analysis, with 52 patients in the intensive group and 52 patients in the more intensive group. LDL-C levels decreased from 119.7 to 69.5 mg/dL (-38%) with intensive therapy and from 127.4 to 42.5 mg/dL (-65%) with more intensive therapy (between-group P < .001). At 18 months, both TPV and NCPV decreased in both groups, with significantly greater regression in the more intensive-therapy group. TPV was reduced by -69.8 mm3 (-21.1%) with more intensive therapy vs -39.0 mm3 (-13.6%) with intensive therapy (between-group difference, -30.9 mm3; 95% CI, -57.2 to -4.5 mm3; P = .02), and NCPV was reduced by -82.3 mm3 (-28.2%) vs -53.5 mm3 (-20.0%), respectively (between-group difference, -28.9 mm3; 95% CI, -53.2 to -4.6 mm3; P = .02). CPV increased similarly in both groups. Regression of TPV occurred in 90% of patients receiving more intensive therapy compared with 76% receiving intensive therapy (47 of 52 [90%] vs 38 of 51 [75%]; P = .05), and regression of NCPV was observed in 98% vs 77% (51 of 52 [98%] vs 39 of 51 [77%]; P =.001). Lower achieved LDL-C levels were linearly associated with greater regression of TPV and NCPV.
CONCLUSIONS AND RELEVANCE: This secondary analysis of the FLOWPROMOTE randomized clinical trial demonstrated that in statin-naive patients with CAD, more intensive lipid-lowering therapy was associated with significantly greater regression of total and noncalcified coronary plaque burden compared with intensive therapy. The extent of plaque regression was related to achieved LDL-C levels, supporting the potential for partial reversal of coronary atherosclerosis with intensive lipid reduction.
TRIAL REGISTRATION: ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT04737408.

candidates.title: Assessment of Ototoxicity in Patients With Heart Failure Receiving High-Dose IV Loop Diuretics.
candidates.abstract:
IMPORTANCE: Concern for ototoxicity hinders loop diuretic (LD) dosing in heart failure (HF); given the mechanism by which LDs affect the ear, high-dose LDs should produce transient, not permanent, hearing changes.
OBJECTIVE: To measure the association of LD dose with permanent and temporary ototoxicity.
DESIGN, SETTING, AND PARTICIPANTS: Cohort 1 received a randomized sequence of LD doses (bumetanide, 1.25-10 mg) across study visits with serial audiometry assessments. Cohort 2 received serial LD up to furosemide 500-mg doses during a HF hospitalization with audiometry at baseline and prior to discharge. Cohort 3 retrospectively characterized clinically diagnosed ototoxicity in HF hospitalizations was defined using International Statistical Classification of Diseases and Related Health Problems, Tenth Revision (ICD-10) codes. Cohorts 1 and 2 were single center, while cohort 3 was multicenter. Cohort 1 studied outpatient participants with stable HF, while cohort 2 (n = 40) and cohort 3 studied hospitalized patients with acute HF.
EXPOSURE: Intravenous LD.
MAIN OUTCOMES AND MEASURES: The primary outcomes were clinically diagnosed ototoxicity and hearing changes via audiometry.
RESULTS: Cohort 1 contained 50 participants, cohort 2 contained 40 participants, and cohort 3 contained 22 656 participants. In cohort 1, mean (SD) participant age was 63.2 (10.4) years, and 21 of 50 participants (42%) were women. In cohorts 1 and 2, clinically diagnosed ototoxicity was not observed. In cohort 1, at peak diuretic concentration, worsening hearing shifts were infrequent (24 ears of 400 doses [6%]) but were more common with higher doses (odds ratio [OR], 1.99; 95% CI, 1.21-3.28 per doubling dose; P = .007). Within hours, hearing shifts largely resolved and were absent in 98% of measurements (393 ears of 400 doses). No significant association between LD dose and hearing shifts was present at any time aside from peak LD concentration. In cohort 2, hearing shifts were not different across groups divided by the median daily LD dose and were not associated with LD dose (OR, 1.19; 95% CI, 0.71-1.98 per doubling dose; P = .52). In cohort 3, 608 HF hospitalizations (2.7%) had clinically diagnosed ototoxicity. In multivariable analyses, peak dose of 160 mg furosemide equivalents or greater (OR, 0.83; 95% CI, 0.52-1.31; P = .43) and 400 mg furosemide equivalents or greater (OR, 1.28; 95% CI, 0.71-2.31; P = .41) were not associated with greater clinically diagnosed ototoxicity risk relative to less than 160 mg.
CONCLUSIONS AND RELEVANCE: In this analysis of 2 small HF cohorts, short-term exposure to high-dose LD was not associated with permanent ototoxicity, although concomitant ototoxin use was excluded. Future studies are needed to understand the risk of ototoxicity with repeated LD exposure and in broader HF populations.
TRIAL REGISTRATION: ClinicalTrials.gov Identifiers: NCT04481919 and NCT05323487.

candidates.title: Intersection of Patient and Hospital Rurality in Heart Failure Care and Outcomes.
candidates.abstract:
IMPORTANCE: Rural-urban disparities in heart failure (HF) care delivery and outcomes are well documented. However, it remains unclear if differences in outcomes after HF hospitalization are primarily driven by patient rural residence, hospital resources, or both.
OBJECTIVE: To evaluate associations of patient and hospital rurality with quality of care and postdischarge outcomes after hospitalization for HF with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF).
DESIGN, SETTING, AND PARTICIPANTS: This was a retrospective cohort study of Medicare beneficiaries in US hospitals with HFrEF with an index hospitalization from January 1, 2013, to December 31, 2021. Included were Medicare beneficiaries discharged alive after an index hospitalization for HFrEF. Participants were classified as rural patients hospitalized in rural hospitals (rural-rural), rural patients in urban hospitals (rural-urban), urban patients in urban hospitals (urban-urban), and urban patients in rural hospitals (urban-rural). Study data were analyzed from July to September 2026.
EXPOSURES: Patient rural residence and hospital rurality.
MAIN OUTCOMES AND MEASURES: Primary outcome was 90-day all-cause mortality after hospitalization. Secondary outcomes included inpatient cardiology consultation, 90-day postdischarge guideline-directed medical therapy (GDMT) use based on prescription fills, and HF readmission at 30 days, 90 days, and 1 year.
RESULTS: Among 735 460 beneficiaries (median [IQR] age, 77 [70-85] years; 415 077 male [56.4%]), 69 061 (9.4%) were rural-rural, 65 510 (8.9%) rural-urban, 582 947 (79.3%) urban-urban, and 17 942 (2.4%) urban-rural. Compared with rural patients treated in rural hospitals, rural patients treated in urban hospitals were more likely to receive inpatient cardiology consultation (odds ratio [OR], 2.02; 95% CI, 1.84-2.22) and initiation of several GDMT classes, including β-blockers (OR, 1.20; 95% CI, 1.16-1.25), ARNIs (OR, 1.23; 95% CI, 1.13-1.34), MRAs (OR, 1.23; 95% CI, 1.15-1.31), and SGLT2Is (OR, 1.48; 95% CI, 1.32-1.67). They also had lower rates of HF readmission and mortality at all time points (HF readmission 1-year: OR, 0.85; 95% CI, 0.82-0.88; mortality 1-year: OR, 0.91; 95% CI, 0.89-0.94) than rural-rural patients. Compared with urban patients hospitalized at urban hospitals, rural patients hospitalized at urban hospitals more often received inpatient cardiology consultation (OR, 1.38; 95% CI, 1.31-1.44), whereas postdischarge GDMT differences were modest (absolute difference in GDMT score 0.09 points; 95% CI, 0.05-0.14). Rural patients also had lower HF readmission (1-year OR, 0.81; 95% CI, 0.79-0.82) but higher 30- and 90-day mortality than urban patients (30-day OR, 1.10; 95% CI, 1.06-1.14; 90-day OR, 1.05; 95% CI, 1.02-1.08).
CONCLUSIONS AND RELEVANCE: Results suggest that hospital rurality was associated with lower odds of GDMT use and higher rates of all-cause mortality, whereas rural residence was associated with mortality differences despite treatment in urban hospitals. Interventions addressing both inpatient resource disparities and postdischarge transitions of care may reduce rural-urban inequities in HF outcomes.

candidates.title: Analysis Asks: Are GLP-1 Drugs Safe in People With Frailty?
Performance of 0/1 h versus 0/3 h pathways in patients with suspected myocardial infarction: a systematic review and individual participant data meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials.
candidates.abstract:
BACKGROUND: In patients with suspected myocardial infarction, the 0/1 h pathway (blood draws at 0 h and 1 h) is recommended in current guidelines for early risk stratification. However, individual trials used different safety outcomes, and efficacy outcomes were inconclusive or not assessed. We conducted a systematic review and individual participant data meta-analysis of all randomised controlled trials to synthesise the totality of the evidence, assess heterogeneity across trials, and evaluate clinically relevant outcomes using harmonised definitions across trials.
METHODS: In this systematic review and individual participant data meta-analysis, we searched PubMed, Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, Scopus, and the International Clinical Trials Registry Platform from inception to July 6, 2026, without language restrictions, for randomised trials comparing the safety and efficacy of 0/1 h versus 0/3 h pathways (blood draws at 0 h and 3 h, ie, standard care). Individual participant data were obtained and outcome definitions were harmonised. The primary analysis used a two-stage random-effects meta-analysis. After receipt of the individual participant data but before data harmonisation or analysis, the primary safety outcome was refined to a composite of all-cause death or new type 1 myocardial infarction within 30 days, from the originally specified composite of all-cause death or any new myocardial infarction. The primary efficacy outcomes were emergency department length of stay and direct discharge from the emergency department. This meta-analysis is registered with PROSPERO (CRD420261383452).
FINDINGS: Our systematic review identified five randomised trials, all of which provided individual participant data. Among these, the definition of the primary safety outcome varied, and in four trials emergency department length of stay was not reported for the whole analysis population. We included 110 933 patient presentations (55 489 managed with the 0/1 h pathway and 55 444 managed with the 0/3 h pathway). Within 30 days, all-cause death or new type 1 myocardial infarction occurred in 446 patient presentations (0·8%) with the 0/1 h pathway versus 562 patient presentations (1·0%) with the 0/3 h pathway (random-effects pooled odds ratio [OR] 0·83 [95% CI 0·45-1·53]; I2=62·9%; τ2=0·143). Emergency department length of stay was 314 min (IQR 211-481) in the 0/1 h pathway group versus 308 min (209-453) in the 0/3 h pathway group (random-effects pooled geometric mean ratio 1·03 [95% CI 0·85-1·25]; I2=99·2%; τ2=0·024). Direct discharge from the emergency department occurred in 37 190 patient presentations (67·0%) with the 0/1 h pathway versus 36 485 patient presentations (65·8%) with the 0/3 h pathway (random-effects pooled OR 1·31 [95% CI 0·79-2·16]; I2=97·8%; τ2=0·156).
INTERPRETATION: Across the available randomised trials, short-term adverse event rates were low with both pathways, but the pooled safety estimate remained imprecise. On average, earlier cardiac troponin retesting did not reduce emergency department length of stay or clearly increase direct discharge, and substantial between-study heterogeneity indicates that treatment effects might not translate uniformly across health-care systems. For hospitals considering transitioning from a 0/3 h to a 0/1 h pathway, implementation decisions should take broader diagnostic and organisational considerations into account.
FUNDING: Swiss National Science Foundation, Swiss Heart Foundation, University Hospital Basel, University of Basel, and Foundation for Cardiovascular Research Basel.

candidates.title: Prone positioning and high-frequency oscillatory ventilation in early paediatric acute respiratory distress syndrome (PROSpect): an international, two-by-two factorial, response-adaptive, phase 3, randomised controlled trial.
candidates.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Data on prone positioning and high-frequency oscillatory ventilation (HFOV) used separately or in combination in patients with paediatric acute respiratory distress syndrome (PARDS) are inconclusive, leading to wide practice variability. We aimed to compare the effects of prone positioning with supine positioning and the effects of HFOV with conventional mechanical ventilation on ventilator-free days in children with early, moderate-to-severe PARDS.
METHODS: PROSpect was an international, two-by-two factorial, response-adaptive, phase 3, randomised controlled trial done in 75 paediatric intensive care units in 18 countries. Eligible patients were aged 2 weeks to 20 years, and were intubated and mechanically ventilated for less than 96 h before meeting criteria for moderate-to-severe PARDS. Patients were centrally randomly assigned using a web-based system to supine positioning and conventional mechanical ventilation, prone positioning and conventional mechanical ventilation, supine positioning and HFOV, or prone positioning and HFOV. Initially, the allocation was 1:1:1:1 stratified by age group and direct or indirect lung injury using a permuted block design with blocks of four and eight. Response-adaptive randomisation updates were planned to adjust allocation probabilities 28 days after 300 patients were randomly assigned and then 28 days after every 100 additional patients. Given the nature of the interventions, masking was not possible. The primary outcome was ventilator-free days through to day 28 among all randomly assigned participants. Safety was assessed prospectively by daily monitoring for the occurrence of prespecified adverse events. This study was registered with ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT03896763) and is closed to enrolment.
FINDINGS: Between May 1, 2019 and Jan 13, 2026, 1045 patients were eligible for enrolment. The trial was stopped early for futility and slow enrolment after 424 of 600 planned patients were recruited. 126 patients were randomly assigned to the supine and conventional mechanical ventilation group, 130 to the prone and conventional mechanical ventilation group, 90 to the supine and HFOV group, and 78 to the prone and HFOV group. Median age was 3·3 years (IQR 1·1-10·1), 211 (50%) patients were female, and 213 (50%) were male. There were no significant differences in ventilator-free days between prone and supine positioning (median 17·9 days [IQR 8·9-21·3] vs 17·4 days [6·4-21·9]; Hodges-Lehmann location shift adjusting for ventilation 0·0 [95% CI -0·8 to 1·0]) or between HFOV and conventional mechanical ventilation (17·3 [5·7-21·6] vs 18·0 [9·9-21·5]; Hodges-Lehmann location shift adjusting for positioning -0·3 [95% CI -1·5 to 0·5]). 41 (10%) patients had died at day 28, without group differences. Plugging or obstruction of the artificial airway occurred more frequently with prone than supine positioning (14 events in 12 [6%] of 188 patients vs three events in three [2%] of 197 patients; 0·74 [95% CI 0·44-1·26] vs 0·15 [0·05-0·47] events per 100 artificial airway days; rate ratio 4·83 [95% CI 1·38-16·82]). Stage 2 or worse immobility-related pressure injuries also occurred more frequently with prone versus supine positioning (12 [6%] vs two [1%]; relative risk 6·13 [95% CI 1·45-25·97]). Haemodynamic instability occurred more frequently with HFOV than conventional mechanical ventilation (41 events in 19 [13%] of 141 patients vs 38 events in 22 [9%] of 244 patients; 2·21 [95% CI 1·63-3·00] vs 1·22 [0·89-1·68] events per 100 paediatric intensive care unit days; rate ratio 1·84 [95% CI 1·18-2·87]). One serious adverse event, an unwitnessed self-extubation followed by cardiopulmonary arrest, occurred in a patient in the prone and conventional mechanical ventilation group.
INTERPRETATION: We found no evidence to support prone positioning or HFOV as first-line strategies to improve ventilator-free days in patients with early, moderate-to-severe PARDS. Thus, the routine use of these strategies in this population is not recommended.

candidates.title: Impact of obesity on clinical outcomes and the treatment effect of catheter ablation in atrial fibrillation: insights from CABANA.
candidates.abstract:
AIMS: Obesity and atrial fibrillation (AF) are global epidemics, often co-existing and compounding cardiovascular risk. While catheter ablation has emerged as an effective strategy for rhythm control in symptomatic AF, it remains unclear whether obesity modifies its benefit. This post hoc analysis of the CABANA trial investigates the influence of baseline obesity on clinical outcomes after catheter ablation vs. drug therapy in AF patients.
METHODS AND RESULTS: A total of 2170 CABANA participants with available body mass index (BMI) were included. Obesity was defined by BMI ≥ 30 kg/m2, and Class II obesity by BMI ≥ 35 kg/m2. Adverse outcomes, AF recurrence, and functional status were analysed using Cox, mixed-effects, and generalized estimating equation models, assessing treatment-by-obesity interactions. Obese patients exhibited higher comorbidity burden, worse baseline functional status, and more persistent AF compared to non-obese counterparts. Higher BMI was associated with increased cardiovascular hospitalization and a higher New York Heart Association functional class. Catheter ablation significantly reduced the risk of AF recurrence and improved symptom burden and functional capacity, irrespective of obesity status. No significant interaction was found between BMI and treatment effect on the primary composite endpoint of cardiovascular hospitalization or all-cause mortality. However, patients with Class II obesity or higher had worse absolute outcomes despite similar relative benefits from ablation.
CONCLUSION: While obesity is associated with worse baseline status and outcomes, it was not shown to significantly alter the relative effectiveness of AF ablation compared to drug therapy. These findings support a multifaceted approach integrating rhythm control with upstream interventions targeting obesity-related atrial remodelling and comorbidity management.

candidates.title: Impact of obesity on procedural safety and 1-year outcomes after pulsed-field ablation for atrial fibrillation.
candidates.abstract:
AIMS: Obesity is associated with atrial fibrillation (AF), atrial remodelling, and cardiometabolic comorbidities. Whether baseline body mass index (BMI) influences procedural safety and effectiveness of pulsed-field ablation (PFA) remains uncertain. We evaluated the association of baseline BMI with procedural characteristics, periprocedural safety, and 1-year arrhythmia recurrence after first-time PFA for AF.
METHODS AND RESULTS: FRANCE-PFA is a nationwide registry including consecutive patients undergoing first-time AF ablation with a pentaspline PFA catheter. Patients with available BMI were categorized as <25, 25 to <30, 30 to <35, or ≥35 kg/m2. Periprocedural complications and 1-year atrial arrhythmia recurrence were assessed across BMI categories. Among 5223 patients, BMI was available in 4573 (87.6%). Higher BMI was associated with greater cardiometabolic burden, more persistent AF, larger atria, and more extensive ablation strategies, including fewer pulmonary vein isolation-only procedures and more additional lesion sets (all P < 0.001). Periprocedural complications remained infrequent (1.0%), with no significant difference across BMI categories. At 1 year, recurrence was driven mainly by AF type rather than obesity. Within paroxysmal and non-paroxysmal AF, recurrence rates were comparable between patients with BMI < 35 and ≥35 kg/m2 (13.8% vs. 9.1% and 22.9% vs. 23.3%, respectively; log-rank P = 0.925). Severe obesity was not associated with recurrence after multivariable adjustment (HR, 0.86; 95% CI, 0.65-1.14; P = 0.299), with similar findings when BMI was analysed continuously.
CONCLUSION: In this nationwide PFA cohort, higher BMI identified a more advanced AF phenotype and more extensive ablation strategies but was not independently associated with periprocedural complications or 1-year arrhythmia recurrence.

candidates.title: Levodopa or dopamine agonists for enhancing motor function after stroke.
candidates.abstract:
RATIONALE: Stroke is a leading cause of mortality and disability worldwide. There is a lack of evidence regarding pharmacological enhancement of stroke recovery with dopamine agonists or levodopa, in particular in terms of motor deficits.
OBJECTIVES: To assess the effects of dopaminergic agents, defined as levodopa or dopamine agonists, on improving motor function after stroke.
SEARCH METHODS: We conducted an extensive database search on the Cochrane Stroke Group trials register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, CINAHL, PsycINFO, Science Citation Index Expanded, CPCI-S, BIOSIS Citation Index, ProQuest Dissertation and Theses Global up to November 2025.
ELIGIBILITY CRITERIA: We included randomised controlled trials (RCTs) that enrolled participants with a clinical diagnosis of stroke, irrespective of age or stroke aetiology and without a pre-existing indication for the use of levodopa or dopamine agonists. Eligible trials compared levodopa or dopamine agonists with a comparator group who received placebo or no medication, with equivalent rehabilitative care in both groups, and aimed at enhancing motor function after stroke.
OUTCOMES: Motor function was the critical benefit outcome. As a critical harm outcome, we assessed serious adverse events. Important outcomes consisted of death, recurrent stroke, disability, dependence, health-related quality of life, activities of daily living, total number of adverse events, and psychiatric adverse events.
RISK OF BIAS: Two review authors independently assessed the risk of bias for each trial using the Cochrane Risk of bias tool (RoB 1).
SYNTHESIS METHODS: We synthesised results for each outcome using a standardised mean difference (SMD) or mean difference (MD) for continuous data and risk ratio (RR) for dichotomous results, with a random-effects model due to heterogeneity between the trials. For non-extractable trials due to missing numerical data, we synthesised the results narratively. We used GRADE to assess the certainty of evidence for each outcome.
INCLUDED STUDIES: We included 12 parallel-group RCTs involving 1860 participants. The trials were conducted in Europe, the USA and Asia, and were published between 2001 and 2025. All trials included participants with either ischaemic strokes only or both haemorrhagic and ischaemic strokes. The mean age of all included participants ranged from 55 to 78 years. Of the included trials, 10 were placebo-controlled and two compared levodopa or dopamine agonists against usual care. Eleven trials investigated levodopa as the intervention and one examined the dopamine agonist ropinirole.
SYNTHESIS OF RESULTS: Across 12 included trials, complete data on motor function were available for six trials with continuous data (1258 participants) and for two trials with dichotomous data (615 participants), of which one trial assessed both continuous and dichotomous data. We detected no difference in motor function scores between levodopa or dopamine agonists and the comparator groups for continuous outcomes (SMD 1.42, 95% confidence interval (CI) -0.20 to 3.05; 6 trials, 1258 participants; very low-certainty evidence). The wide confidence intervals indicate substantial imprecision in the effect estimate. Consistent with those results, we detected no difference for dichotomous motor function outcomes either (RR 0.93, 95% CI 0.82 to 1.06; 2 trials, 615 participants; anticipated absolute event rate of having a favourable outcome of 581/1000 in the comparator group versus 540/1000 with levodopa/dopamine agonists; low-certainty evidence). Heterogeneity for the critical outcome motor function (continuously measured) was high (I2 = 99%). However, a sensitivity analysis including only two trials with a low risk of bias in all domains, that accounted for the majority of the included patient population (1025 of 1258), showed no heterogeneity (I2 = 0%), and a smaller confidence interval (SMD 0.02, 95% CI -0.10 to 0.14; 2 trials, 1025 participants), implying no difference between groups. Six trials assessed serious adverse events, including 1281 participants. There was no notable difference in the risk of serious adverse events between groups (RR 1.03, 95% CI 0.83 to 1.27; anticipated absolute event rate of 302/1000 events in comparators versus 311/1000 events with levodopa/dopamine agonists; low-certainty evidence). All important outcomes showed no notable between-group differences. The certainty of evidence, according to GRADE, was very low for continuously measured scores of motor function, low for dichotomous motor function outcomes, and low for serious adverse events. Together with heterogeneity in both interventions and outcomes, inconsistency of findings, imprecision related to small sample sizes in some trials, and imprecision of summary effect, there are major limitations of the current evidence.
AUTHORS' CONCLUSIONS: Based on limited data, we did not find evidence that the use of levodopa or dopamine agonists improves motor function after a stroke. Given the low certainty of evidence due to limited data, wide confidence intervals, and heterogeneity across trials, further research may change this assessment and explore whether effects are different in specific subgroups of patients.

candidates.title: Maternity versus non-maternity healthcare settings for the diagnosis of gestational diabetes or diabetes in pregnancy.
candidates.abstract:
RATIONALE: Substantial uncertainty exists regarding how healthcare system factors, especially care setting types, affect the uptake and implementation of gestational diabetes or diabetes in pregnancy screening in practice. Evidence suggests that the care environment may influence diagnostic processes.
OBJECTIVES: To assess the effectiveness of maternity and non-maternity healthcare settings for the diagnosis of gestational diabetes mellitus or diabetes in pregnancy.
SEARCH METHODS: We searched CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, and Cumulative Index to Nursing and Allied Health Literature (CINAHL) for randomised controlled trials (RCTs) up to April 2026, and for controlled non-randomised studies of interventions (NRSIs) up to December 2025. We also searched CENTRAL to identify ongoing trials.
ELIGIBILITY CRITERIA: We included RCTs and planned to include cluster-RCTs and NRSIs, but we did not find any. Eligible participants were pregnant women being screened for gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM) or diabetes in pregnancy. We defined maternity healthcare settings as those specialising in care for pregnant, birthing, and postpartum individuals, with appropriate screening protocols, and non-maternity healthcare settings as general medical environments lacking a focus on pregnancy and women's care. We considered any screening format (e.g. risk-factor-based screening) and any diagnostic test (e.g. one- and two-step oral glucose tolerance tests (OGTT)).
OUTCOMES: Critical health service outcomes were compliance with screening and follow-up guidelines, diagnosis of gestational diabetes or diabetes in pregnancy, maternal emergency department visits during pregnancy, maternal antenatal hospitalisation, length of maternal hospitalisation, length of neonatal hospitalisation, and care accessibility. Critical maternal outcomes included hypertensive disorders, maternal death, intensive care admissions, hyperglycaemia requiring pharmacological treatment, infections, and postpartum glucose intolerance, including progression to diabetes, within 15 years after birth. Critical child-related outcomes encompassed perinatal death, neonatal intensive care admissions, preterm birth, neonatal hypoglycaemia, large-for-gestational-age, shoulder dystocia, and birth trauma. Further critical and important outcomes not included in the summary of findings tables can be found in the full text.
RISK OF BIAS: We used the Cochrane RoB 2 tool to assess bias in the RCTs. We had planned to use ROBINS-I version 2 to assess bias in the NRSIs if we had identified any.
SYNTHESIS METHODS: We used standard Cochrane methodology. We planned to synthesise results for each outcome using meta-analysis where possible (inverse-variance or Mantel-Haenszel approaches; fixed-effect model). We used GRADE to assess the certainty of the evidence for each outcome.
INCLUDED STUDIES: We included one RCT with 781 participants: 390 were randomised to screening in a maternity healthcare setting and 391 were randomised to screening in a non-maternity healthcare setting. Except for screening compliance, trialists evaluated all outcomes using a per-protocol analysis instead of by original randomised groups. This approach created substantial disparities in sample sizes between settings and largely nullified the methodological protections typically provided by a randomised design. The trial evaluated screening for GDM only. We did not identify any ongoing studies or studies awaiting classification.
SYNTHESIS OF RESULTS: Health service outcomes Screening in a maternity healthcare setting may increase compliance with screening and follow-up guidelines (risk ratio (RR) 1.69, 95% confidence interval (CI) 1.53 to 1.87; 781 participants) and may improve care accessibility, assessed as time to access antenatal diabetes care, measured in days (mean difference (MD) -4.70, 95% CI -6.03 to -3.37; 690 participants), both with low-certainty evidence. We are very uncertain about the effect of screening in a maternity healthcare setting versus a non-maternity healthcare setting on diagnosis of gestational diabetes or diabetes in pregnancy (RR 1.10, 95% CI 0.60 to 2.01; 690 participants; very low-certainty evidence) and length of neonatal hospitalisation (MD 0.04, 95% CI -0.57 to 0.65; 690 participants; very low-certainty evidence). No direct evidence was available on screening for diabetes in pregnancy as distinct from GDM. No data were reported on maternal emergency department visits, maternal antenatal hospitalisation, length of maternal hospitalisations, and costs. Maternal outcomes We are very uncertain about the effect of screening in a maternity healthcare setting versus a non-maternity healthcare setting on pre-eclampsia (RR 1.24, 95% CI 0.56 to 2.75; 690 participants; very low-certainty evidence). The following outcomes were not reported: eclampsia, HELLP syndrome, maternal death, admission to intensive care, hyperglycaemia requiring pharmacological treatment, infections, and postpartum glucose intolerance. Child-related outcomes We are very uncertain about the effect of screening in a maternity healthcare setting versus a non-maternity healthcare setting on: stillbirth or foetal death (RR 0.91, 95% CI 0.08 to 9.93), admission to neonatal intensive care (RR 1.01, 95% CI 0.59 to 1.71), preterm birth (RR 1.06, 95% CI 0.41 to 2.71), neonatal hypoglycaemia (RR 0.91, 95% CI 0.23 to 3.59), large-for-gestational-age (RR 0.73, 95% CI 0.51 to 1.04), shoulder dystocia (RR 0.15, 95% CI 0.01 to 3.70), and birth trauma (RR 0.91, 95% CI 0.08 to 9.93), all with 690 participants each and very low-certainty evidence. An effect estimate for neonatal death was not estimable (maternity setting: 0/475; non-maternity setting: 0/215).
AUTHORS' CONCLUSIONS: There is insufficient evidence to determine whether screening for gestational diabetes or diabetes in pregnancy in maternity healthcare settings compared with non-maternity healthcare settings improves health service, maternal, or child-related outcomes. Low-certainty evidence from a single study indicates that screening in maternity healthcare settings may result in a reduction in time to access antenatal diabetes care and may increase compliance. The effects on other outcomes remain unknown. Conducting studies using intention-to-treat analyses could bridge existing research gaps, enhancing effect estimates and certainty.
FUNDING: This Cochrane review was funded by the World Health Organization (WHO) and the UNDP-UNFPA-UNICEF-WHO-World Bank Special Programme of Research, Development and Research Training in Human Reproduction (HRP).

candidates.title: Clopidogrel Versus Aspirin Monotherapy According to Atherothrombotic Risk Profile.
candidates.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Clopidogrel monotherapy has shown superior efficacy compared with aspirin after completion of dual antiplatelet therapy following percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI). However, whether treatment effects differ according to overall atherothrombotic risk integrating clinical and angiographic factors remains unclear.
METHODS: This post hoc analysis of the SMART-CHOICE 3 (Smart Angioplasty Research Team: Choice of Optimal Anti-Thrombotic Strategy in Patients Undergoing Implantation of Coronary Drug-Eluting Stents 3) randomized trial included patients who completed guideline-directed dual antiplatelet therapy after PCI. Atherothrombotic risk was defined using the a Thrombolysis in Myocardial Infarction Risk Score for Secondary Prevention and complex PCI. Patients with Thrombolysis in Myocardial Infarction Risk Score for Secondary Prevention ≥3 or complex PCI were classified as higher risk, and those with a Thrombolysis in Myocardial Infarction Risk Score for Secondary Prevention <3 without complex PCI were classified as lower risk. The primary end point was major adverse cardiac and cerebrovascular events (death, myocardial infarction, or stroke). Bleeding was defined as Bleeding Academic Research Consortium type 2, 3, or 5.
RESULTS: Among 5506 patients, 4486 (81.5%) were at higher risk and 1020 (18.5%) were at lower risk. Over a median 2.3 years, the incidence of major adverse cardiac and cerebrovascular events was higher in the higher-risk group (6.1% versus 3.1%; hazard ratio, 1.83 [95% CI, 1.17-2.78]; P=0.007). In higher-risk patients, clopidogrel reduced major adverse cardiac and cerebrovascular events compared with aspirin (4.6% versus 7.4%; hazard ratio, 0.67 [95% CI, 0.50-0.89]; P=0.006), with no difference in lower-risk patients (3.0% versus 3.2%; hazard ratio, 1.03; P=0.945; interaction P=0.242). Bleeding was similar between groups.
CONCLUSIONS: After completion of dual antiplatelet therapy following PCI, clopidogrel monotherapy was associated with lower ischemic risk than aspirin in patients with higher atherothrombotic risk, without increased bleeding.

candidates.title: Right Atrial Phasic Function Improves CMR-Based Prognostication in Patients with Heart Failure with Mildly Reduced Ejection Fraction: A Multicenter Study.
candidates.abstract:
AIMS: In multiple cardiovascular diseases, right atrial (RA) function can serve as an independent predictor for the clinical status and prognosis. However, the prognostic value of RA strain in patients with heart failure with mildly reduced ejection fraction (HFmrEF) remains considerably unknown. This study aims to explore the relationships between RA strain derived from cardiac magnetic resonance imaging-feature tracking (CMR-FT) and adverse outcomes in patients with HFmrEF.
METHODS AND RESULTS: This retrospective study enrolled patients with HFmrEF who were referred for echocardiography and CMR at two tertiary medical centers from April 2016 to September 2024. The primary endpoint was a composite of all-cause mortality, HF-related hospitalization and cardiac transplantation. The findings were validated in a cohort of patients with HFmrEF enrolled from two additional tertiary care centers (January 2019 to January 2025). The development cohort included 1317 patients, and the validation cohort comprised 385 patients. During a median follow-up period of 2.8 years and 2.1 years, respectively, 243 and 72 patients in the development cohort and validation cohort reached the primary endpoint, respectively. Cox regression analysis showed that RA conduit strain was an independent predictor of the primary outcome (HR: 0.86 [0.82, 0.90]; P < .001). The full model integrating clinical variables, traditional imaging, and RA strain achieved the best predictive performance (C-index: 0.80 in development, 0.81 in validation cohorts).
CONCLUSION: RA conduit strain derived from CMR is an independent predictor of adverse outcomes in patients with HFmrEF, providing incremental prognostic value beyond traditional clinical and imaging-derived risk markers.​.

candidates.title: Left Bundle-Branch Area Pacing vs Right Ventricular Pacing for Atrioventricular Block and Preserved Left Ventricular Function: The LEAP-Block Randomized Clinical Trial.
candidates.abstract:
IMPORTANCE: For patients with atrioventricular block requiring high-burden ventricular pacing, the optimal pacing strategy to reduce heart failure (HF) and all-cause mortality remains uncertain. Robust comparative evidence on the clinical outcomes of left bundle-branch area pacing (LBBAP) vs right ventricular pacing (RVP) in this population is needed.
OBJECTIVE: To compare 24-month clinical outcomes of LBBAP vs RVP in patients with atrioventricular block and preserved left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF; ≥50%).
DESIGN, SETTING, AND PARTICIPANTS: The LEAP-Block study was a prospective, multicenter, randomized, controlled, superiority trial conducted across 14 Chinese hospitals from January 2021 to August 2025, with last follow-up on June 3, 2025. Of 551 patients with LVEF 50% or greater requiring ventricular pacing who underwent eligibility assessment, 499 with anticipated ventricular pacing greater than 40% were randomized.
INTERVENTIONS: Patients were randomized in a 1:1 ratio to LBBAP (n = 249) or RVP (n = 250).
MAIN OUTCOMES AND MEASURES: The primary end point was a composite of all-cause death, HF events, or upgrade to biventricular pacing at 24 months. Secondary end points included pacing-induced cardiomyopathy and device-related complications.
RESULTS: The primary analysis included 482 patients (LBBAP, n = 242; RVP, n = 240; mean age, 67 years; 46% female). Acute procedure success was comparable between the 2 groups (LBBAP, 237/242 [97.9%] vs RVP, 239/240 [99.6%]; P = .22), with left bundle-branch capture confirmed in 188 of 236 patients (79.7%). LBBAP significantly reduced the primary end point vs RVP (2.4% vs 12.5%, respectively; absolute risk difference, -10.1% [95% CI, -16.8% to -3.4%]; P = .003). Among secondary outcomes, the LBBAP group had fewer HF events (3.4% vs 11.3%; -7.9% [95% CI, -13.0% to -2.8%]). No significant differences were observed in all-cause death, biventricular pacing upgrade, device-related complications, or pacing-induced cardiomyopathy. The 24-month Kaplan-Meier estimated cumulative incidence of the primary end point was 5.0% for LBBAP vs 13.2% for RVP (hazard ratio, 0.37 [95% CI, 0.19 to 0.73]; P = .004). LBBAP superiority was consistent across all prespecified subgroups.
CONCLUSIONS AND RELEVANCE: Among patients with atrioventricular block and preserved LVEF requiring high-burden ventricular pacing, LBBAP was superior to RVP in reducing the risk of the composite end point of all-cause death, HF events, or upgrade to biventricular pacing at 24 months.

candidates.title: Prediction and Risk Stratification for 30-Day Mortality in Stable Acute Pulmonary Embolism: Recalibration of the Multimarker Calculator and Evaluation of the AHA/ACC Classification.
candidates.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Risk stratification in haemodynamically stable acute pulmonary embolism (PE) remains challenging. The multimarker calculator (MMC) provides individualized 30-day mortality estimates, whereas the 2026 AHA/ACC Acute PE Clinical Categories (AHA/ACC classification) provide a phenotype-based framework incorporating clinical severity, right ventricular dysfunction, cardiac biomarker elevation, and respiratory compromise. We evaluated these approaches and recalibrated the original MMC in a Chinese multicentre cohort.
METHODS: We included adults with haemodynamically stable acute PE from the prospective, multicentre China pUlmonary thromboembolism REgistry Study (2012-2021). The primary outcome was 30-day all-cause mortality. The MMC, 2019 European Society of Cardiology (ESC) model, and AHA/ACC classification were assessed using discrimination, decision-curve analysis, risk classification, and subgroup analyses. Logistic recalibration updated the original MMC linear predictor. The AHA/ACC classification was evaluated using 7-, 4-, and simplified phenotype-based 3-category schemes.
RESULTS: Among 11,568 patients, 331 died within 30 days (2.9%). The MMC and 7-category AHA/ACC classification showed better discrimination than the ESC model (AUC, 0.704 and 0.680 vs. 0.606). The original MMC overestimated intermediate-high-risk mortality (mean predicted risk, 16.2%; observed risk, 9.4%). Recalibration improved calibration and identified a smaller intermediate-high-risk subgroup comprising 2.2% of patients, with 13.2% observed mortality. In the 3-category AHA/ACC classification, mortality increased stepwise across category B, partial phenotype involvement, and dual cardiopulmonary phenotype involvement (0.7%, 2.7%, and 6.7%).
CONCLUSIONS: The recalibrated MMC may be useful for individualized 30-day mortality risk estimation, whereas the AHA/ACC classification may offer a simple framework for phenotype-based risk grouping.

candidates.title: Prediction of All-Cause Mortality, Cardiovascular Mortality, and Angiographic Coronary Disease From LVEF Reserve: Findings From the Multicenter REFINE PET Registry.
candidates.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Left ventricular ejection fraction reserve (LVEF-R), defined as stress EF minus rest EF, is a marker for high-risk coronary artery disease in patients undergoing positron emission tomography myocardial perfusion imaging, but its prognostic and diagnostic significance in large real-world populations remains incompletely defined. We aimed to analyze the association of LVEF-R with mortality and high-risk obstructive coronary artery disease in a large multicenter cohort.
METHODS: We analyzed 34 976 patients from 13 sites who underwent gated rest and vasodilator stress positron emission tomography myocardial perfusion imaging from the Registry of Flow and Perfusion Imaging for Artificial Intelligence with PET. Associations between LVEF-R and all-cause mortality and cardiovascular death were assessed using multivariable Cox regression models. In a subset with invasive coronary angiography (n=6843), the relationship between LVEF-R and angiographic disease was evaluated.
RESULTS: A total of 9392 (26.9%) patients had an LVEF-R<0%. Over a median follow-up of 4.1 years, lower LVEF-R demonstrated a graded association with higher mortality. Compared with LVEF-R>5%, adjusted hazard ratios for all-cause mortality were 1.20 for LVEF-R 0% to 5% ([95% CI, 1.13-1.28]; P<0.001), 1.32 for -5% to 0% ([95% CI, 1.23-1.42]; P<0.001), and 1.38 for ≤-5% ([95% CI, 1.24-1.52]; P<0.001). A negative LVEF-R was also associated with high-risk coronary artery disease, including left main and 3-vessel disease.
CONCLUSIONS: LVEF-R is an independent predictor of mortality, with a graded association between impaired reserve and adverse outcomes. A negative LVEF-R identifies patients with a higher likelihood of multivessel or left-main coronary artery disease, supporting its role as a clinically relevant marker of high-risk disease.

candidates.title: Cortisol in cardio-kidney-metabolic disease.
candidates.abstract: Despite guideline-directed therapy, many patients with cardio-kidney-metabolic (CKM) disease remain uncontrolled due to therapeutic inertia, adherence barriers, and underrecognized secondary causes. Hypercortisolism, ranging from mild autonomous cortisol secretion (MACS) to overt Cushing syndrome, is an increasingly recognized contributor. MACS is associated with a 2.5-fold higher risk of cardiovascular death and increased prevalence of hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM), and kidney impairment. Cortisol excess promotes muscle insulin resistance, hepatic gluconeogenesis, β-cell dysfunction, sodium retention, and vascular remodelling, worsening glycaemia and blood pressure, leading to poor CKM outcomes. Recent prospective studies suggest that hypercortisolism is more prevalent than previously suspected in selected CKM phenotypes, including 24% in patients with difficult-to-control T2DM in CATALYST and 27% in patients with resistant hypertension in MOMENTUM. The overnight 1 mg dexamethasone suppression test remains the diagnostic test of choice. Therapeutic strategies include adrenal steroidogenesis inhibitors, glucocorticoid receptor antagonists, and pituitary-directed therapies in selected cases, while surgery remains the first-line treatment for surgically remediable disease. This review summarizes the epidemiology and mechanisms linking cortisol excess to CKM dysfunction, and also highlights the need for clinical trials, standardized diagnostic thresholds, and assays to enable integration of cortisol-targeted therapies into management pathways to mitigate residual CKM risk. This review will serve as a practical guide for cardiologists to manage a potentially reversible contributor to poor CKM control.

candidates.title: Waitlist Outcomes of Multiorgan Heart Transplant Candidates.
candidates.abstract:
BACKGROUND: In recent years, the number of patients undergoing simultaneous multiorgan heart transplant (MOT) has increased significantly. However, there is no unified policy for MOT allocation, allowing Organ Procurement Organizations to individually determine priority for match runs across all organ types. We evaluated if heart transplant (HT) candidates listed simultaneously for a kidney or liver are at a disadvantage on the waitlist.
METHODS: Adult HT candidates registered with the Scientific Registry of Transplant Recipients between 2019-2023 were included. Candidates were waitlisted statuses 1-6 within the heart allocation system in order of medical urgency. The primary outcomes were transplantation and removal from the waitlist for death or clinical deterioration, estimated with cumulative incidence functions for the first-year after listing, stratified by both waitlist status and type of organ listing. Rates of transplantation and removal from the waitlist at 1 year were reported. Using cox proportional hazards models, cause-specific hazards of transplantation and removal, holding waitlist status constant were estimated.
RESULTS: Of 20,588 HT candidates, 9.3% were heart kidney (HK) and 1.4% were heart liver (HL) candidates. Irrespective of status, heart-alone candidates had higher cumulative incidence of transplant (70.6% vs. 67.9% HK, p < 0.01; vs. 63.6% HL, p < 0.01), and lower cumulative incidence of removal from the waitlist for death or deterioration (5.3% vs. 10.3%, p < 0.01); vs. 10.4%, p < 0.01). In adjusted analysis and stratified by candidate listing center, MOT listing was significantly associated with lower likelihood of transplant (HK: HR 0.71, 0.68-0.75; HL: HR 1.13, 1.09-1.17), and a significantly higher risk of delisting due to death or deterioration (HK: HR 2.08, 1.81, 2.39; HL: HR 2.45, 1.75, 3.42). Hemodialysis-dependent HK candidates experienced the highest cumulative incidence of death or deterioration at 1 year (13%) compared to non-hemodialysis dependent (8.7%, p < 0.01) and heart-alone (5.3%, p < 0.01) candidates, but similar to HL candidates (10.4%, p = 0.32).
CONCLUSION: MOT candidates, especially HK, had worse waitlist outcomes with lower rates of transplantation and higher incidence of removal from the waitlist compared to heart-alone candidates. These outcomes demonstrate a need for MOT allocation based on criteria more reflective of medical urgency.

candidates.title: Preoperative Predictors of Outcome for Adults Undergoing Congenital Cardiac Surgery: Multicenter Model Validation.
candidates.abstract:
OBJECTIVE: Adults with congenital heart disease (ACHD) undergoing cardiac surgery represent a growing population in whom conventional surgical risk models perform suboptimally. We externally validated a previously described ACHD-specific preoperative risk model and evaluated whether performance could be improved through recalibration/model updating.
METHODS: We conducted a prospective, multicenter observational study of patients ≥16 years undergoing congenital cardiac surgery at four centers (March 2020-April 2023). The primary composite adverse outcome (CAO) comprised in-hospital death, prolonged ventilation >7 days, or new-onset dialysis. We evaluated discrimination and calibration of the original preoperative model (including MELD-XI, cognitive impairment, body-mass index [BMI], prior chest wall incisions, and complex anatomy) and then performed bootstrap-based model updating (200 resamples) to derive refined models with and without the Adult Congenital Heart Surgery (ACHS) procedural mortality score.
RESULTS: Among 538 patients, CAO occurred in 4.3% (n=23). In external validation (n=383 complete cases), the original model preserved discrimination (AUC=0.729, 95% confidence interval: 0.602-0.855) but systematically overestimated risk, indicating need for recalibration. The refined model retained BMI, prior chest incisions, cognitive impairment, age, serum albumin level, and ventricular systolic dysfunction. Discrimination was good without procedural complexity (AUC=0.799; 0.697-0.900) and improved with inclusion of the ACHS score (AUC=0.857; 0.779-0.935).
CONCLUSIONS: In this prospective multicenter external validation, an ACHD-specific preoperative risk model maintained discrimination but required recalibration. Incorporating procedural complexity enhanced discrimination, supporting a hybrid patient- and procedure-based approach to guide perioperative planning.

candidates.title: Chronic Impact of Cavo-Tricuspid Isthmus Ablation on the Adjacent Right Coronary Artery: The IMPACT-CTI Study.
candidates.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Relative to radiofrequency ablation (RFA), pulsed field ablation (PFA) raises concerns regarding chronic coronary narrowing when energy is delivered adjacent to coronary arteries. Because PFA can provoke acute coronary vasospasm, many operators employ RFA near coronary vessels, although the comparative long-term coronary effects of PFA vs RFA are unknown.
OBJECTIVES: The purpose of this study was to compare the chronic impact of cavotricuspid isthmus (CTI) ablation with PFA vs RFA vs no CTI ablation on the adjacent right coronary artery (RCA) and to explore factors associated with progressive RCA narrowing.
METHODS: This single-center retrospective registry included consecutive patients undergoing atrial fibrillation ablation who received CTI ablation with PFA or RFA or received no CTI ablation (control) and who had baseline and follow-up coronary computed tomography (CT) angiography, with blinded assessment of the RCA segment adjacent to the CTI. The primary endpoint was a ≥10% reduction in RCA caliber from baseline to the last available follow-up CT, analyzed as an event rate; ≥20% reduction and progression to clinically significant stenosis were secondary assessments. Continuous change in RCA dimension over follow-up was analyzed secondarily.
RESULTS: In total, 155 patients were included: 39 PFA, 59 RFA, and 57 control. The mean age was 69.7 ± 9.6 years, 45% were women, and 55% had coronary artery disease (CAD). CTI block was achieved in all ablation patients. For the primary endpoint, assessed from baseline to the last available follow-up CT, RCA narrowing ≥10% occurred in 12.8%, 15.3%, and 3.5% for PFA, RFA, and control patients, respectively (PFA vs RFA risk difference -2.4%; 95% CI: -15.8% to +13.1%); ≥20% narrowing occurred in 7.7%, 13.6%, and 3.5%, respectively. Mean change in RCA dimension at last CT was -4.7 ± 8.4%, -5.9 ± 11.1%, and -2.9 ± 7.0% for PFA, RFA, and control patients, respectively (secondary continuous analysis PFA vs RFA P = 0.29); median changes were -2.4% (Q1-Q3: -2.9% to 0.0%), -2.5% (Q1-Q3: -2.9% to 0.0%), and -2.4% (Q1-Q3: -2.7% to 0.0%), respectively. No patient progressed to clinically significant (≥70%) stenosis or experienced ischemic events. RCA narrowing occurred exclusively among patients with baseline CAD. In the CTI ablation cohort, ≥10% narrowing occurred in 21.9% with CAD vs 0% without CAD (P = 0.002). Sensitivity analyses stratified by CAD and restricted to first-time AF ablation did not materially change the observed PFA-vs-RFA comparison.
CONCLUSIONS: PFA (with prophylactic intravenous nitroglycerin) and RFA of the CTI produced modest, subclinical changes in the adjacent RCA, with no clinically significant stenosis; rates of RCA narrowing did not differ significantly between energy sources, but the study was not powered to establish equivalence. Progressive RCA narrowing occurred only in patients with baseline coronary disease. Larger studies are needed to establish comparative coronary safety.

candidates.title: NT-proBNP and Clinical Outcomes in Patients With HFrEF According to Atrial Fibrillation: Insights From QUEST.
candidates.abstract:
BACKGROUND: The Chinese traditional medicine qiliqiangxin (QLQX) improves outcomes in patients with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF) when added to guideline-directed medical therapy.
OBJECTIVES: This post hoc analysis of the QUEST (Qiliqiangxin in Heart Failure: Assessment of Reduction in Mortality) trial assessed the efficacy and safety of QLQX according to baseline N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide (NT-proBNP) levels, and examined whether the prognostic value of baseline NT-proBNP varied by atrial fibrillation (AF) status.
METHODS: QUEST enrolled 3,110 patients with HFrEF and NT-proBNP ≥450 pg/mL, and followed them for a median of 18 months. The primary outcome was cardiovascular (CV) death or heart failure (HF) hospitalization. NT-proBNP was analyzed by quartiles and as a continuous variable.
RESULTS: Median baseline NT-proBNP was 1,731 pg/mL. Higher baseline NT-proBNP independently predicted greater risk of the primary outcome (adjusted HR for Q4 vs Q1: 4.03 [95% CI: 3.12-5.20]). The prognostic value of baseline NT-proBNP for all outcomes was consistent irrespective of AF status. At 3 months, QLQX reduced NT-proBNP by 10% compared with placebo. The HRs for the primary composite with QLQX vs placebo were 1.13 (95% CI: 0.73-1.76), 0.76 (95% CI: 0.54-1.06), 0.73 (95% CI: 0.55-0.95), and 0.75 (95% CI: 0.59-0.95) from the lowest to the highest NT-proBNP quartiles, respectively (Pinteraction = 0.48). Results were consistent for CV death, HF hospitalization, and total HF hospitalizations, and when NT-proBNP was modeled continuously (all Pinteraction ≥ 0.30).
CONCLUSIONS: The treatment effect of QLQX on CV events was consistent across the spectrum of baseline NT-proBNP in HFrEF. Baseline NT-proBNP strongly predicted the risk of CV outcomes and mortality, irrespective of AF status. (Qiliqiangxin in Heart Failure: Assessment of Reduction in Mortality [QUEST]; ChiCTR1900021929).

candidates.title: Transcriptomics Identifies a Small Set of Circulating Biomarkers and Signaling Pathways Dysregulated in Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy.
candidates.abstract:
BACKGROUND: It is sometimes challenging to distinguish hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM) from other cardiomyopathies with left ventricular hypertrophy (LVH). At present, no circulating biomarkers to distinguish HCM have been established.
OBJECTIVES: The authors aimed to identify plasma microRNA (miRNA) biomarkers unique to HCM.
METHODS: In this multicenter case-control study, the authors performed comprehensive plasma transcriptomics profiling in cases with HCM and controls with hypertensive LVH, transthyretin amyloid cardiomyopathy (ATTR-CM), and aortic stenosis (AS). For each disease group, they chronologically split the patients into training and test sets. The authors identified miRNAs that were significantly (Benjamini-Hochberg-adjusted P < 0.05) upregulated or downregulated in HCM compared with hypertensive LVH. They made the same comparisons between HCM and ATTR-CM and between HCM and AS. They determined miRNAs that were consistently upregulated or downregulated in HCM throughout all 3 comparisons. Then, they selected miRNAs independently associated with HCM after adjusting for potential confounders. Using the selected miRNAs, the authors developed a logistic regression model to distinguish HCM in the training set. They calculated the area under the receiver-operating characteristic curve in the test set.
RESULTS: The authors analyzed 2,656 miRNAs in patients with HCM (n = 294), hypertensive LVH (n = 321), ATTR-CM (n = 167), and AS (n = 38). They identified 3 miRNAs (miR-454-3p, miR-98-5p, and miR-5581-3p). The logistic regression model using the 3 miRNAs had an area under the receiver-operating characteristic curve of 0.95 (95% CI: 0.93-0.97) with a sensitivity of 0.95 and a specificity of 0.90 in the test set.
CONCLUSIONS: Comprehensive plasma transcriptomics profiling identified a small set of circulating miRNAs to distinguish HCM from other cardiomyopathies with LVH.

candidates.title: Liver Extracellular Volume in Patients With Tricuspid Regurgitation: A Novel Prognostic Marker.
candidates.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Liver extracellular volume (L-ECV), a novel cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR) parameter of systemic venous congestion, might help to stratify tricuspid regurgitation (TR) patients at higher risk, but its role in this context is unexplored.
OBJECTIVES: The aim of this study was to assess the incremental prognostic relevance of L-ECV in a large TR cohort.
METHODS: Data were collected from patients with TR referred to CMR between 2019 and 2024 who had parametric mapping analysis for L-ECV quantification. The primary endpoint was the composite of all-cause mortality and heart failure (HF) hospitalization, under medical management.
RESULTS: In 462 patients included (median age: 67 years; 43% female), median left ventricular ejection fraction was 51% (Q1-Q3: 40%-59%), median tricuspid regurgitant fraction was 21% (Q1-Q3: 14%-33%), and median L-ECV was 31% (Q1-Q3: 28%-35%). When dividing the cohort according to median L-ECV value, patients with high L-ECV (≥ median) showed worse baseline status with more clinical and imaging signs of right HF and (after a median follow-up of 2.1 years) poorer survival free from the primary outcome (P < 0.001) compared with patients with low L-ECV. High L-ECV independently predicted the outcome even after multivariable adjustment accounting for TR severity, biventricular ejection fraction, and pulmonary pressure (adjusted HR: 1.82; 95% CI: 1.03-3.18; P = 0.030). Finally, L-ECV showed incremental prognostic value compared with TRI-SCORE when assessed in a nested Cox model.
CONCLUSIONS: In our large real-world TR cohort, L-ECV appeared as a novel, powerful CMR marker of right HF with an independent and incremental prognostic value to stratify patients with TR at higher risk of events.

candidates.title: Embolization of the middle meningeal artery for non-acute subdural hematoma.
candidates.abstract: This is a protocol for a Cochrane review (intervention). The objectives are as follows: To evaluate the benefits and harms of the embolization of the middle meningeal artery for non-acute subdural hematoma in adults. Secondary objectives To assess equity-related issues, including sex and gender, through subgroup analyses comparing the intervention's effects between male and female subjects, between younger and older adults, and across different pre-event functional status.
